input.question: How do we actually know the age of the Earth? (Repost)
input.ground_truth: Elements like uranium and thorium are unstable and they decay into elements which are not stable themselves and so on. This is called a radioactive cascade or decay chain. Since these elements existed prior to the formation of the solar system, we can determine the ratios of the end products and knowing the decay rates of the decay chain, calculate how long ago the rock was formed. When we do this what we measure is *not* the age of the elements but of the rock itself because when rock is formed, most of the final elements of the decay chain can escape and the radiodating process is 'reset'.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: How do we actually know the age of the Earth? (Repost)

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine you have a big, old birthday cake, and you want to know how many candles you need to put on it to show how old it is.

Scientists can’t just count the candles on the Earth because it doesn’t have any! But they are really smart, so they use clues to figure out how old the Earth is.

One way is like looking at layers in a cake. The Earth has layers inside it, like rocks and minerals. By looking at these layers and seeing how they stack up, scientists can guess how long it took for them to form, kind of like counting the layers of a cake to guess how many years it took to bake.

Another way is like watching a sand timer. There are some special rocks on Earth and in space (like from the Moon!) that have tiny clocks inside them. These clocks are called “radiometric clocks.” Over time, these clocks tick at a certain speed, and by looking at how much they’ve ticked, scientists can figure out how old the rocks are. Some of these rocks are almost as old as the Earth itself!

So, by putting all these clues together—like counting cake layers and reading special clocks—scientists can tell that the Earth is about 4 and a half billion years old! That’s a really, really, REALLY long time!
